OK I want a new tool to build for myself. The idea is this - it should be cross agents - it should work for both codex and claude code. Then, I want a unified place where I can see all my sessions, and be able to reliably, easily send them over to anyone. I saw this interesting piece where if I copy and paste them from a terminal into firefox, I should be able because of rich text to see exactly the session from my terminal in a browser.

But then, I want this to be in a way automated. What options do we have tof rosmething like this? Are there options out there already available for something like this? I don't want to make it commercial in any way

You want a local-first session layer that sits above both agents, preserves terminal fidelity, and makes sessions easy to browse, export, and hand off. I’m checking two things in parallel: what Codex/Claude Code already expose officially, and which existing open-source terminal/session tools can be reused instead of building the whole stack.

As of March 17, 2026, there still isn’t one obvious open-source tool that fully does “Codex + Claude Code + unified browser + reliable portable handoff” end to end. But there are enough pieces that you probably should not start from zero.

**Existing Options**
- [Agent Sessions](https://github.com/jazzyalex/agent-sessions) is the closest existing session hub. It’s local-first, MIT-licensed, and can browse/search/resume Codex CLI and Claude Code sessions together. The main limitation is that it’s a native macOS app, not a portable share/export system.
- [AI Sessions MCP](https://github.com/yoavf/ai-sessions-mcp) is a strong cross-agent building block. It reads native local session stores for Claude and Codex and exposes them through MCP, so either agent can search old sessions from the other. It is MIT-licensed.
- [LunaRoute](https://github.com/erans/lunaroute) is the best “automatic capture” option I found. It is an Apache-2.0 local proxy for both Anthropic and OpenAI traffic, records sessions to SQLite + JSONL, and gives you a web UI. If you want future sessions auto-recorded across both tools, this is the cleanest path.
- [claude-code-log](https://github.com/daaain/claude-code-log) is very good for Claude-only export. It produces HTML/Markdown, has a TUI, and is MIT-licensed. It’s a good reference implementation for the rendering/export side.
- [asciinema](https://docs.asciinema.org/getting-started/) is still the best terminal-native replay format. It is open source, self-hostable, embeddable, and its player supports copyable text. It’s great for “show exactly what happened in the terminal,” but it records terminal I/O, not higher-level agent semantics.
- [terminal-to-html](https://github.com/buildkite/terminal-to-html) is a useful ANSI-to-HTML renderer if your main goal is rich, self-contained browser output from terminal sessions.

**What I’d Recommend**
- Build on native session files first, not on clipboard tricks. Claude officially exposes `session_id` and `transcript_path` in its [status line integration](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/statusline), and supports [resume flows](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/tutorials). Codex is clearly storing local history too; community tools and open issues work directly from `~/.codex/sessions`, and OpenAI says the [Codex app picks up session history from the CLI](https://openai.com/index/introducing-the-codex-app/).
- Make the core artifact a self-contained HTML export plus JSON and Markdown. That is the reliable handoff format. The browser/clipboard path should be a convenience feature, not the source of truth.
- If you want full automation for new sessions, add a second capture mode: either proxy-based with [LunaRoute](https://github.com/erans/lunaroute) or PTY-based with [asciinema](https://docs.asciinema.org/getting-started/).
- If you only want value quickly, you could combine [Agent Sessions](https://github.com/jazzyalex/agent-sessions) for browsing with [AI Sessions MCP](https://github.com/yoavf/ai-sessions-mcp) for cross-agent access, then add your own exporter on top.

**Important Caveat**
- I would not trust Firefox rich-text copy as the canonical transport. Mozilla discussions and bugs show clipboard HTML/style behavior is inconsistent, especially when styling comes from external CSS rather than inline styles. Use exported HTML with inline styling; add “Copy as HTML” on top if you want, but don’t base the system on that. Sources: [Mozilla discussion](https://discourse.mozilla.org/t/copy-rich-text-from-firefox-does-not-capture-style/97862), [Bugzilla](https://bugzilla.mozilla.org/show_bug.cgi?id=705560).
- Codex still appears to lack a polished native export feature; there are open requests for [session transcripts/export](https://github.com/openai/codex/issues/2765) and [copy/export as Markdown](https://github.com/openai/codex/issues/2880).

ok hear me out now - what about if I'm in the terminal let's say, and I have a mac wide system shortcut - cmd + option + ctrl + c. I invoke that, the following triggers:

* the tool checks the app that is in foreground
* it can check the tab that is open, and the type of agent in there - claude code or codex
* then, it takes that session (from sessions JSONL file) and uploads it to your github maybe as a gist, as an image and/or transcript
* you are authenticated beforehand with github
* then you already get a URL in your clipboard (pbcopy) to directly share

This is feasible, but the critical decision is where the truth comes from: I’m checking the GitHub/Gist constraints and then I’ll map out the simplest reliable macOS trigger flow versus the parts that will need per-terminal adapters.

Yes. That workflow is viable.

The important shift is this: don’t make the hotkey figure everything out from the visible terminal at share time. Make each agent register its current session while it runs, then let the hotkey resolve and publish that session. That is the reliable version.

**Recommended Design**
1. `Capture`
- Claude Code already gives you `session_id` and `transcript_path` via its local [status line hook](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/statusline). Use that to keep a tiny local registry like `~/.agent-share/active-sessions.json`.
- For Codex, I did not find an equivalent official hook. Community tools read `~/.codex/sessions`, including [Agent Sessions](https://github.com/jazzyalex/agent-sessions) and [AI Sessions MCP](https://github.com/yoavf/ai-sessions-mcp). So for Codex, I’d use a wrapper command or launcher that records `pid`, `tty`, `cwd`, and inferred session file when Codex starts.

2. `Resolve`
- The global shortcut app checks the frontmost app using macOS APIs like [NSWorkspace.frontmostApplication](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/appkit/nsworkspace/frontmostapplication).
- If it’s a supported terminal, use either Accessibility/UI scripting ([Apple guide](https://developer.apple.com/library/archive/documentation/LanguagesUtilities/Conceptual/MacAutomationScriptingGuide/AutomatetheUserInterface.html), [AXUIElement](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/applicationservices/axuielement_h)) or a terminal-specific API.
- Inference: generic “which tab/pane/session is active?” is flaky across terminals. Per-terminal adapters are better. If you standardize on iTerm2 first, this gets much easier because it has a real [tab/session API](https://iterm2.com/python-api/tab.html).

3. `Export`
- Generate three artifacts:
  - `transcript.md`
  - `session.json`
  - `terminal.html`
- Make `terminal.html` the main share artifact: inline CSS, terminal colors, code blocks, timestamps, maybe collapsible tool calls. This is better than relying on Firefox rich-text paste.

4. `Publish`
- Use [GitHub CLI](https://cli.github.com/manual/gh_gist_create) with prior `gh auth login`.
- Default to a secret gist. `gh gist create` already supports that.
- Copy the resulting URL with `pbcopy`.

**One Important Constraint**
- GitHub’s official [Gist REST API](https://docs.github.com/en/rest/gists/gists) models files as text `content` strings. That makes “upload transcript + image via gist API” awkward.
- So I would not make PNG the default.
- Better defaults:
  - self-contained `terminal.html`
  - `transcript.md`
  - `session.json`
- If you really want a visual asset, emit an SVG “terminal snapshot” or use a private repo instead of a gist.

**Best Implementation Paths**
- Fast MVP: Hammerspoon or Raycast + shell scripts + `gh`.
- Best long-term: a tiny Swift menu bar app with a global shortcut, Accessibility permission, and agent adapters.
- Lowest-risk MVP scope:
  - support only `iTerm2`
  - support Claude first, Codex second
  - publish HTML/Markdown/JSON only
  - secret gist only
  - clipboard URL only

**Why This Is Better Than Clipboard/Rich Text**
- Firefox paste fidelity is not a stable transport.
- A generated HTML artifact is deterministic, shareable, searchable, and works the same later.
- You also avoid having to scrape the visible terminal buffer.

**Existing Pieces Worth Reusing**
- [Agent Sessions](https://github.com/jazzyalex/agent-sessions): parser/reference for Codex and Claude local session stores.
- [AI Sessions MCP](https://github.com/yoavf/ai-sessions-mcp): cross-agent session access model.
- [terminal-to-html](https://github.com/buildkite/terminal-to-html): ANSI to HTML rendering reference.

If you want, I can turn this into a concrete MVP spec next: local registry format, hotkey flow, supported terminals, and a first-cut file layout for the tool.

The idea is this - I want to be able to copy current session via a single command, and then the flow completes and I get a URL. That's the entire thing. That other person when they open the URL, it should render the session. Then we can upload it to my personal website then?

I’m narrowing this to the single-command path now. The main question is whether the share target should be a gist or a page on your own site, because that determines whether the URL opens as a real rendered session page or just a file viewer.

Yes. Uploading to your personal website is the right version of this.

If the requirement is:

1. press one shortcut
2. current agent session gets exported
3. a URL lands in your clipboard
4. the other person opens it and sees a rendered session

then the share target should be a self-contained HTML page on your site, not a gist.

Why:
- Gists are fine for raw text, but they are a poor fit for “open URL and see a rendered session page.”
- Your site gives you stable URLs, full control over rendering, nicer UX, and easier cleanup/search later.
- GitHub Pages supports custom domains and static HTML directly, so this can stay non-commercial and cheap: [GitHub Pages custom domains](https://docs.github.com/pages/configuring-a-custom-domain-for-your-github-pages-site/about-custom-domains-and-github-pages), [configuring custom domains](https://docs.github.com/pages/configuring-a-custom-domain-for-your-github-pages-site).

The clean architecture is:

- A local command, for example `agent-share current`
- A global macOS shortcut calls that command
- The command resolves the active session
- It reads the session transcript
- It renders `index.html` for that session
- It uploads that page to `https://yourdomain.com/sessions/<id>/`
- It copies that URL with `pbcopy`

For session detection:
- Claude Code has an official hook path here: its status line can expose `session_id` and `transcript_path`, which is ideal for keeping a live registry of the active session: [Claude Code status line](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/statusline)
- Inference: I did not find an equivalent official Codex hook, so for Codex I would use a small launcher/wrapper and local registry keyed by `pid`/`tty`/`cwd`, then resolve the current terminal tab against that registry at share time.

So the simplest reliable MVP is:

- Support `iTerm2` first
- Support `Claude Code` first, `Codex` second
- Generate one self-contained HTML file per session
- Publish to a `sessions/` section of your personal site
- Copy the final canonical URL

Best deployment options:
- Easiest public path: a GitHub Pages repo on your custom domain
- Cleaner long-term path: a small upload endpoint on your site that accepts the generated HTML/JSON and writes it under `/sessions/`
- If you want “unlisted but shareable,” use hard-to-guess URLs; if you want real privacy, add auth or signed links

So: yes, this is absolutely buildable, and “personal website first” is better than “gist first.”

- publish pipeline
- session HTML schema
- macOS shortcut implementation options (`Hammerspoon`, `Raycast`, or a small Swift app)
and it should look like in the terminal, can we do that? I don't want us to reinvent the wheel

I’m checking the rendering side specifically now. The constraint is whether the source data actually contains terminal styling; if it does, we can reuse a player/renderer and get very close without building our own terminal renderer.

Yes, but only if we use terminal capture as the source of truth.

If you render from the agent’s session JSONL alone, you’ll get the conversation content, not the exact terminal screen state. For “looks like the terminal,” the best existing wheel to reuse is [asciinema player](https://docs.asciinema.org/manual/player/) with an `.cast` recording. It’s built for terminal replays, embeddable on any HTML page, and can be self-hosted on your site with the standalone JS/CSS bundle: [quick start](https://docs.asciinema.org/manual/player/quick-start/), [embedding](https://docs.asciinema.org/manual/server/embedding/). That also makes it cross-agent by default, because it records the terminal session, not Claude or Codex specifically.

So I’d split the problem like this:

- Best fidelity: `asciinema`
  - Start Codex/Claude through a wrapper that records the terminal from session start.
  - Your hotkey just finds the active recording, uploads the `.cast` plus a tiny HTML page to your site, and copies the URL.
  - This gives you replay, copyable text, and a view that actually feels like the terminal.

- Best on-demand fallback: `terminal-to-html`
  - If a session was not recorded from the start, dump the terminal buffer and convert ANSI output to static HTML with [terminal-to-html](https://github.com/buildkite/terminal-to-html).
  - This is good for “share what I’m looking at right now,” but it’s a snapshot, not a replay.

My recommendation is a hybrid MVP:
- Primary path: `asciinema` for real sessions.
- Fallback path: `terminal-to-html` for already-running sessions.
- Optional metadata: attach Claude/Codex transcript JSONL for search/indexing, but don’t use it for the visual rendering.

That avoids reinventing the renderer entirely. You’d only be building:
- the macOS shortcut trigger
- active-session resolution
- upload-to-site step
- URL copy step

Yes. With the Maccy-style workflow, this gets simpler.

You do not need to inspect the foreground app or tab anymore. The launcher can just index the native Claude/Codex session files, show them in a Maccy-like chooser, and let you act on any session. Then `Cmd+1` can mean “publish selected session”, upload a self-contained page to your site, and put the final URL into the clipboard so `Cmd+V` works anywhere.

The right way to do this without reinventing everything is:
- Reuse existing Claude/Codex session parsing and indexing from tools like [Agent Sessions](https://github.com/jazzyalex/agent-sessions), [agentsview](https://www.agentsview.io/), or [agent-session-viewer](https://pypi.org/project/agent-session-viewer/). `agent-session-viewer` is especially close to your goal because it already reads both stores and exports self-contained HTML.
- Build only the missing layer: a native macOS picker with Maccy-like UX plus a “publish to my site” action.
- Render the shared page in a terminal style. If you want the browser page to feel like a terminal, use something like [xterm.js](https://github.com/xtermjs/xterm.js) for the presentation layer, or just a static terminal-themed HTML template.

One important limitation: from the JSONL alone, you can make it look like a terminal, but you cannot reconstruct the exact terminal screen state pixel-for-pixel. The JSONL is a semantic transcript, not a screen recording. For your workflow, that is probably fine. You’ll get a terminal-looking transcript page, which is the right tradeoff. If you later want exact replay, that becomes a separate recording problem.

For the local UX, I would not try to extend Maccy itself. I’d build a separate tiny app with the same interaction model. Fast prototype: [Hammerspoon `hs.chooser`](https://www.hammerspoon.org/docs/hs.chooser.html). Better long-term version: a small Swift/AppKit popup.

The MVP I’d recommend is:
- global hotkey opens chooser
- chooser lists recent Claude/Codex sessions from a local index
- `Cmd+1` publishes selected session
- publisher generates one self-contained `index.html`
- it uploads to `your-site/sessions/<slug>/`
- URL is copied with `pbcopy`

One practical note: if your personal site is on GitHub Pages, publishing may not be instant because there is a deploy step. If you want the URL live immediately, use a direct upload target on your site instead of a git-based deploy.

Claude’s official [status line hook](https://docs.anthropic.com/en/docs/claude-code/statusline) is useful too, because it exposes `session_id` and `transcript_path`, which makes indexing cleaner.

# claude-code-transcripts

[![PyPI](https://img.shields.io/pypi/v/claude-code-transcripts.svg)](https://pypi.org/project/claude-code-transcripts/)
[![Changelog](https://img.shields.io/github/v/release/simonw/claude-code-transcripts?include_prereleases&label=changelog)](https://github.com/simonw/claude-code-transcripts/releases)
[![Tests](https://github.com/simonw/claude-code-transcripts/workflows/Test/badge.svg)](https://github.com/simonw/claude-code-transcripts/actions?query=workflow%3ATest)
[![License](https://img.shields.io/badge/license-Apache%202.0-blue.svg)](https://github.com/simonw/claude-code-transcripts/blob/main/LICENSE)

Convert Claude Code session files (JSON or JSONL) to clean, mobile-friendly HTML pages with pagination.

[Example transcript](https://static.simonwillison.net/static/2025/claude-code-microjs/index.html) produced using this tool.

Read [A new way to extract detailed transcripts from Claude Code](https://simonwillison.net/2025/Dec/25/claude-code-transcripts/) for background on this project.

> [!WARNING]
>
> The `web` commands for both listing Claude Code for web sessions and converting those to a transcript are both broken right now due to changes to the unofficial and undocumented APIs that these commands were using. See [issue #77](https://github.com/simonw/claude-code-transcripts/issues/77) for details.

## Installation

Install this tool using `uv`:
```bash
uv tool install claude-code-transcripts
```
Or run it without installing:
```bash
uvx claude-code-transcripts --help
```

## Usage

This tool converts Claude Code session files into browseable multi-page HTML transcripts.

There are four commands available:

- `local` (default) - select from local Claude Code sessions stored in `~/.claude/projects`
- `web` - select from web sessions via the Claude API
- `json` - convert a specific JSON or JSONL session file
- `all` - convert all local sessions to a browsable HTML archive

The quickest way to view a recent local session:

```bash
claude-code-transcripts
```

This shows an interactive picker to select a session, generates HTML, and opens it in your default browser.

### Output options

All commands support these options:

- `-o, --output DIRECTORY` - output directory (default: writes to temp dir and opens browser)
- `-a, --output-auto` - auto-name output subdirectory based on session ID or filename
- `--repo OWNER/NAME` - GitHub repo for commit links (auto-detected if not specified). For `web` command, also filters the session list.
- `--open` - open the generated `index.html` in your default browser (default if no `-o` specified)
- `--gist` - upload the generated HTML files to a GitHub Gist and output a preview URL
- `--json` - include the original session file in the output directory

The generated output includes:
- `index.html` - an index page with a timeline of prompts and commits
- `page-001.html`, `page-002.html`, etc. - paginated transcript pages

### Local sessions

Local Claude Code sessions are stored as JSONL files in `~/.claude/projects`. Run with no arguments to select from recent sessions:

```bash
claude-code-transcripts
# or explicitly:
claude-code-transcripts local
```

Use `--limit` to control how many sessions are shown (default: 10):

```bash
claude-code-transcripts local --limit 20
```

### Web sessions

Import sessions directly from the Claude API:

```bash
# Interactive session picker
claude-code-transcripts web

# Import a specific session by ID
claude-code-transcripts web SESSION_ID

# Import and publish to gist
claude-code-transcripts web SESSION_ID --gist
```

The session picker displays sessions grouped by their associated GitHub repository:

```
simonw/datasette              2025-01-15T10:30:00  Fix the bug in query parser
simonw/llm                    2025-01-14T09:00:00  Add streaming support
(no repo)                     2025-01-13T14:22:00  General coding session
```

Use `--repo` to filter the session list to a specific repository:

```bash
claude-code-transcripts web --repo simonw/datasette
```

On macOS, API credentials are automatically retrieved from your keychain (requires being logged into Claude Code). On other platforms, provide `--token` and `--org-uuid` manually.

### Publishing to GitHub Gist

Use the `--gist` option to automatically upload your transcript to a GitHub Gist and get a shareable preview URL:

```bash
claude-code-transcripts --gist
claude-code-transcripts web --gist
claude-code-transcripts json session.json --gist
```

This will output something like:
```
Gist: https://gist.github.com/username/abc123def456
Preview: https://gisthost.github.io/?abc123def456/index.html
Files: /var/folders/.../session-id
```

The preview URL uses [gisthost.github.io](https://gisthost.github.io/

    """Extract plain text from message content.

    Handles both string content (older format) and array content (newer format).

    Args:

    Returns:
        The extracted text as a string, or empty string if no text found.
    """
    if isinstance(content, str):
        return content.strip()
    elif isinstance(content, list):
        # Extract text from content blocks of type "text"

        for block in content:

        return " ".join(texts).strip()
    return ""

def detect_github_repo(loglines):
    """
    Detect GitHub repo from git push output in tool results.

    Looks for patterns like:
    - github.com/owner/repo/pull/new/branch (from git push messages)

    Returns the first detected repo (owner/name) or None.
    """
    for entry in loglines:
        message = entry.get("message", {})
        content = message.get("content", [])
        if not isinstance(content, list):

        for block in content:
            if not isinstance(block, dict):

            if block.get("type") == "tool_result":
                result_content = block.get("content", "")
                if isinstance(result_content, str):

**What’s Worth Reusing**
- The repo already has the exact basic pipeline you need: scan local Claude sessions, let the user pick one, generate static HTML, optionally publish it. See the local picker and publish flow in [the CLI code](https://github.com/simonw/claude-code-transcripts/blob/main/src/claude_code_transcripts/__init__.py#L1519).
- It normalizes both `.jsonl` and `.json` into one internal shape before rendering. That is the right pattern for your cross-agent tool too: `claude adapter -> normalized session`, `codex adapter -> normalized session`.
- The output is self-contained HTML with inline CSS/JS, pagination, search, tool-specific rendering, and embedded images. That part is reusable in spirit even if you change the visual design. The rendering macros are in [templates/macros.html](https://github.com/simonw/claude-code-transcripts/blob/main/src/claude_code_transcripts/templates/macros.html).
- The one-command publish path is simple and pragmatic: generate files, then call `gh gist create`. See [create_gist()](https://github.com/simonw/claude-code-transcripts/blob/main/src/claude_code_transcripts/__init__.py#L1251).
- The testing approach is solid. For a renderer like this, snapshot tests are the right choice. Simon explicitly calls that out in the article.

**What Not To Copy**
- The current UI is `questionary` in a terminal, not a native macOS popup. That is fine for a CLI, but it is not your Maccy-style workflow.
- The visual output is “clean transcript cards”, not “looks like a terminal”. It is better for understanding, but it does not match your stated goal.

My recommendation is: use this repo as a reference implementation and probably vendor small parts of the parser/render pipeline, but do not fork it as your main base. The app shape you want is different enough that a clean new project with borrowed ideas will age better.
